title: Two consonants at the start of a word

steps.text: English lets none of these start a word, and where it took one from Greek it went quiet on the first letter: the p of “psalm” and “pneumonia”, the g of “gnome”, the m of “mnemonic”, the p of “pterodactyl”; and an x at the start of an English word is a z, as in “xylophone”. Greek says every letter, wherever it stands: ψυχή starts with ps, πνεῦμα with pn, ξένος with ks.

You say each pair already, inside an English word: ps in “lips”, ks in “box”, pt in “apt”, kt in “act”, mn in “gymnast”, pn in “top note”. Say the word, then the pair alone, then put the Greek vowel after it: “lips”, ps, ψυχή. γν is the soft throaty γ, then n.
Listen for the first letter: it is always there. πνεῦμα, ψυχή and ψεύστης start with a p, ξύλον and κτίσις with a k, γνῶσις with the soft γ, πτωχός with a p, μνημεῖον with an m.

In the first two pairs the second word is the first with the cluster's first letter dropped, as English would drop it: say both letters, or you have said another word. In the last two ξ stands against σ and ζ: it is always ks, never s or z.
Say each word after the voice, with every letter of the start: p and n in πνεῦμα, p and s in ψυχή, k and s in ξύλον. Slip no vowel in between: πνεῦμα has two syllables, not three.
Test the spirits: πνεύματι and πνεύματα, then ψευδοπροφῆται, false prophets, each cluster marked. Hear it, then say it, with the p of every πν and ψ.
